extracted.intended_audience: Congressional staff, federal procurement officials, DOD managers, and policymakers interested in OMB Circular A-76 and competitive sourcing
extracted.subtask_short: OMB Circular A-76 competitive sourcing rules
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the procedural requirements, statutory constraints, and policy criteria governing public‑private competitions and conversion of federal commercial activities under OMB Circular A‑76 (including DOD implementation and related legislation). Intended to guide evaluation, implementation, protest rights, and reporting for competitive sourcing actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive sourcing process requirements (OMB Circular A-76)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an activity is selected for Circular A-76 review, the agency is required to first develop a performance work statement and quality assurance plan. It then issues a request for proposals or invitation for bids from the private sector. As industry develops proposals, the agency puts together a more efficient organization for retaining the work in‑house and prepares its own proposal. The best‑value contract offer is compared with the agency’s proposal to determine final award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must prepare a PWS and QAP, solicit private sector proposals, develop a Most Efficient Organization (MEO) and agency tender, then perform a formal comparison between the contractor offer and the agency MEO/offer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractor award threshold (10% or $10 million savings rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The contractor’s offer must be at least 10% or $10 million below the government’s offer to be awarded the contract. Otherwise, the savings are not deemed significant enough to outsource.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This numeric threshold is the statutory/administrative test used in many instances to judge whether outsourcing yields sufficiently significant savings to justify conversion to contractor performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: commercial activity vs inherently governmental
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'commercial activity' is a not inherently governmental good or service that can be obtained from the private sector (examples: photography, data processing, management support services). An inherently governmental activity 'intimately relates to the public interest,' including activities that require the exercise of discretion in applying government authority or the making of value judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these definitions when deciding whether an activity is subject to FAIR inventories and A-76 review; inherently governmental activities should generally remain performed by government personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOD sourcing decision factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Defense competitive sourcing decisions are usually based on one of three factors: (1) whether the work activity or function is considered 'core' to the mission or component; (2) whether the function has been identified as 'inherently governmental' according to the rules of OMB Circular A-76; and (3) how the function is coded on the FAIR Act inventory (FAIRNET).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these three criteria when screening and prioritizing activities for public‑private competition within DOD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency Tender Official (ATO) duties and characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agency Tender Official (ATO) shall (1) be an inherently governmental agency official with decision‑making authority; (2) comply with this circular; (3) be independent of the contracting officer (CO), source selection authority (SSA), source selection evaluation board (SSEB), and performance work statement (PWS) team; (4) develop, certify, and represent the agency tender; (5) designate the most efficient organization (MEO) team after public announcement of the standard competition; (6) provide the necessary resources and training to prepare a competitive agency tender; and (7) be a directly interested party. An agency shall ensure that the ATO has access to available resources (e.g., skilled manpower, funding) necessary to develop a competitive agency tender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATO must be organizationally independent from acquisition officials, have authority and resources to prepare an agency tender, and act as a directly interested party in protests/competitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: ATO standing to protest (GAO >65 positions rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: GAO issued a final rule which allows the Agency Tender Official (ATO) in charge of the agency’s competitive sourcing bid to file a protest before GAO if the OMB Circular A‑76 competition involved more than 65 positions. If the ATO decides not to file a protest, no other employee representative has the standing to file a protest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impact: federal employees do not have standing to file protests in competitions when there are 65 or fewer positions involved; unions may not file protests on behalf of employees. Employees may intervene if a protest is filed by a third party or a losing bidder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest and evaluator impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations must be reasonable and free from conflicts of interest — GAO found an evaluation process 'fundamentally flawed as a result of a conflict of interest' where many evaluators held positions that were under study as part of the A-76 study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure evaluators do not have disqualifying interests in the matter under evaluation; conduct meaningful discussions and reasonable evaluations to avoid GAO protest reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: OGE Section 208 exemption applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: In accordance with 18 U.S.C. § 208(b)(2), OGE has provided an exemption for such employees who participate in particular matters where the disqualifying financial interest arises from Federal Government employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OGE interpretation may allow participation by certain federal employees despite apparent conflicts tied to their government positions; however, applicability should be assessed case by case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel recommendations and sourcing benchmark principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commercial Activities Panel recommended: (1) the adoption of ten sourcing principles as a benchmark against which to measure sourcing decisions; (2) the abolishment of OMB Circular A-76, replacing it with an 'integrated competition process' that combines elements of the Circular with the Federal Acquisition Regulations (FAR); (3) implementation of limited changes to the Circular that do not require legislation; and (4) the development of federal agencies into high‑performing organizations (HPOs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should consider adopting standardized sourcing principles/benchmarks and moving toward an integrated FAR‑based competition process per panel guidance (subject to statutory limits for DOD).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 335 implementation issues (required considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 335 identified six issues that affect implementation of the revised Circular: (1) the extent to which the revised circular will ensure that DOD employees will have the opportunity to compete to return their jobs; (2) the extent to which the revised circular provides appeal and protest rights to DOD employees; (3) the extent to which safeguards will be identified that would ensure fairness and meet requirements of full and open competition; (4) an implementation plan to phase in the use of the new circular; (5) training on the revised circular of DOD employees, including employee selection for training, funding for training, and the numbers of employees likely to receive training; and (6) data collection and analysis on the results of the revised circular, including costs, quality of work, how much work is contracted out or retained in‑house, and other post‑competition requirements and objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation plans/assessments should explicitly address each of these six elements and collect data to evaluate outcomes post‑competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory constraint on DOD procurements (10 U.S.C. §2462 cost requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 10 U.S.C. § 2462(a), the Secretary of Defense shall procure each supply or service from a private sector source if such a source can provide it at a cost that is lower (after including any cost differential required by law, Executive order, or regulation) than the cost at which the Department can provide the same supply or service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOD decisions are legally constrained to be cost‑based (not 'best value') unless otherwise provided by law; cost comparisons must include required cost differentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: P.L. 108-287 (FY2005 Appropriations) limits on conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: P.L. 108-287 provides limits on the conversion to contractor performance of any activity or function in DOD that, as of enactment, is performed by 11 or more DOD civilian employees unless: (1) the conversion is based on a public‑private competition involving an MEO; (2) the MEO’s personnel‑related costs [are] 10% or $10 million less than that of the contractor; and (3) the contractor offers a bid proposal that requires less of a financial contribution toward the premium share of the DOD health benefits for civilian employees, compared to the amount paid by DOD for health benefits under 5 U.S.C. Chapter 89.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large conversions (11+ employees) must meet these three statutory conditions before conversion to contractor performance is permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 326/327 protest and cost comparison authorities under FY2005 DOD Authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: P.L. 108-375 (FY2005 DOD Authorization Act) grants the agency tender official (ATO) authority to serve as an 'interested party' and file a protest on behalf of federal employees, unless the ATO determines there is no reasonable basis for protest. Section 327 requires that DOD include a formal cost comparison during public‑private competitions, and that there must be a cost‑savings of ' $10 million or 10%' before activities performed by federal employees can be converted to performance by a private contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATO has explicit protest standing under the Authorization Act, and formal cost comparisons with statutory savings thresholds are required for conversion decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAIR Act inventory and reporting requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The FAIR Act (P.L. 105-270) requires agencies to submit inventories of their commercial activities to OMB. FAIR Act inventories are lists compiled by agencies of the commercial activities performed by their employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must classify activities as 'commercial' or 'inherently governmental' and maintain FAIR inventories (e.g., via FAIRNET) as the basis for selecting activities for competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB competitive sourcing reporting metrics and activity categories
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB’s competitive sourcing reports compile information reported annually by federal agencies on completed and announced competitions (e.g., number of FTEs competed, competitions awarded to MEO vs contractor, and estimated savings). Types of activities competed include finance and accounting, environment, procurement, social services, health services, repair & maintenance, depot repair, base maintenance/multi‑function contracts, R&D/test & evaluation, installation services, logistics, education and training, communications and IT services, and minor construction/real property maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these standard activity categories and metrics (FTEs competed, awards to MEO vs contractor, estimated savings) when preparing or evaluating competitive sourcing reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of A-76 as management tool and political/policy constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bush Administration and agencies viewed OMB Circular A-76 and the FAIR Act as management reform tools to meet competitive sourcing goals (e.g., targets to compete percentages of commercial positions). However, implementation is subject to legislative action, congressional oversight, and statutory limitations (e.g., DOD’s reliance on cost determinations under Title 10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy targets (e.g., percent of positions to be competed) are management objectives but must be balanced against statutory rules, congressional constraints, and oversight findings (e.g., GAO skepticism about projected savings).
